reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: A rare condition combining progressive skeletal hyperostosis (dense, thickened bone) with cutis laxa and growth failure
Skin is loose and wrinkled with prominent veins, contrasting strikingly with the increasingly sclerotic skeleton
Characteristic features include cutaneous syndactyly, proximal symphalangism, enamel hypoplasia and a large head with wide fontanelles
Caused by gain-of-function variants in PTDSS1, which encodes phosphatidylserine synthase 1, a lipid biosynthetic enzyme
Intellectual disability is common, and the progressive cranial and skull-base hyperostosis can compromise cranial nerves
The paradox of lax skin with dense bone is a useful diagnostic clue
Management is supportive, with monitoring for neurological complications of progressive hyperostosis
reference.pathophysiology: Lenz-Majewski syndrome is caused by gain-of-function variants in PTDSS1, the gene for phosphatidylserine synthase 1, which loses normal feedback inhibition and overproduces phosphatidylserine. The resulting disturbance of membrane phospholipid metabolism dysregulates bone and connective tissue cells, driving progressive hyperostosis of the skull and skeleton while simultaneously weakening dermal elastic tissue to produce cutis laxa. Digit anomalies, enamel defects and neurological effects reflect the widespread impact of this metabolic imbalance on developing tissues.
additionalDifferentials: Craniodiaphyseal dysplasia and other sclerosing bone dysplasias
Other syndromic causes of syndactyly and hyperostosis
additionalInvestigations: PTDSS1 sequencing where available, within a skeletal dysplasia panel
Skeletal survey demonstrating progressive hyperostosis and diaphyseal changes
Cranial imaging to assess skull-base thickening and neural foramina
Skin examination and, where needed, dermal histology for elastic tissue
redFlags: Cranial nerve compromise (visual, auditory or facial) from progressive skull-base hyperostosis
Signs of raised intracranial pressure or neural foraminal narrowing
Feeding or airway difficulty from craniofacial changes
reference.prognosis: The condition is progressive; survival into adulthood occurs but morbidity accrues from advancing hyperostosis, intellectual disability and cranial nerve complications, so long-term neurological surveillance is important.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis because the combination of lax skin and dense bone seems contradictory
Mistaking it for another sclerosing bone dysplasia without noting the cutis laxa and digital anomalies
Failing to monitor for cranial nerve compromise as hyperostosis progresses
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: There is no disease-specific drug therapy; management is supportive with structured surveillance for the progressive hyperostosis
Undertake regular neurological and cranial-nerve surveillance with cranial imaging, since skull-base hyperostosis can compress cranial nerves and narrow neural foramina
Refer for neurosurgical decompression when progressive hyperostosis threatens cranial nerves or the skull base
Provide developmental and educational support for intellectual disability
Arrange dental care for enamel hypoplasia and orthopaedic or hand-surgery assessment for syndactyly and digital anomalies
Offer genetic counselling for this dominant PTDSS1-related condition, which usually arises as a de novo variant
